# The base design of the controls

What every control of v4 shares once it has taken the base design: the button, the check box with its two types, the switch, and the input group — input field, select box, multi select box, date time picker — together with the popup worlds they open. The values the controls share live in the `controls` and `controlMenus` maps of `src/assets/styles/layout/_index.scss`, with the reason for each value beside it; a value only one control reads — the switch's width, the tab bar's padding — stands in that control's own files, its reason beside it as well. The mechanics live in the two mixins of `src/assets/styles/inputControl/_index.scss` for the input group, in `button.scss` for the button, in `checkBox.scss` plus `icon/icon.scss` for the check box and in `switch.scss` for the switch. The *why* behind the design is in `decisions/`, listed at the end.

## Two appearances, one per ground

A control never knows which of the palette's colours it sits on. It knows whether that colour makes a light or a dark ground, which it reads from the inherited custom property `--ground` without a prop (`dark-areas.md`), and the base design holds exactly two appearances: one for all light grounds, one for all dark ones. **The pair is a control's answer to the ground it is placed on, not a mode the framework is in** — the framework is light, and a dark ground is a property of one area of the page. The map `$ground` of `src/assets/styles/color/_index.scss` states which palette colours make a dark ground. Every value of the design that differs by ground is stated as a pair in the map, under the keys `dark` (the value for a light ground) and `light` (the value for a dark one) — the pairing the typo sets use as well.

## The pane

A control that sets itself apart from its background rests on a **pane**: a translucent veil of the palette — `structureSilver` over light backgrounds, `offWhite` over dark ones — with an edge a notch denser than the fill, a lit rim along the top, a soft inner glow, and a contact shadow that says the body lies on the surface rather than hovering above it. **The pane is glass, and it is one of two the framework has:** this one, from the `controls` map, is what a control is made of, and every body of the base design is cut from it — the switch's knob, the tab bar's lens, the primary header's marker. The second lives in the `glass` map and belongs to a surface that floats over the page, the cards and the popup menus, which is why it carries a backdrop blur and this one does not. The pane comes in three strengths, one calculation:

| Strength | Who carries it |
|---|---|
| `surface` | the filled button at rest; the clickable section |
| `surfaceTinted` — about half of every ingredient, a tighter contact shadow | the tinted button at rest; every input control at rest; the switch at rest; the contact pane of a placed component |
| `surfaceLocked` — the tinted pane halved once more, without rim and glow | every locked control, whatever it rested on: the filled button thins to `surfaceTinted`, the tinted button, the switch and the input controls to this |

A pane whose fill is a colour of the palette — the switch that is on, the filled or overlaid button with a highlight — is opaque, and the veil's ingredients vanish on it. While such a pane can be used it takes the glass of **`surfaceColored`** instead: an edge that darkens the colour with `primary`, a denser rim and glow, one set for both themes, no fill and no contact shadow of its own. Locked, it takes none of that: `ACTIVE` and `BUSY` keep their colour and lie as flat in the surface as every locked pane, which is what says that they cannot be used. The solid highlight, a plate in `primary`, is the one colour the edge cannot darken and keeps the surface's ingredients (ADR `general-control-colored-pane-carries-its-own-glass.md`).

**The full strength is for what is clicked**: the filled button and the clickable section. Under a press both pull the contact shadow together to `contactPressed` and put the rim out.

**A placed component takes the pane as well, where the content asks for it**: `Section`, `Tabular`, `DataTable`, `ValueField` and `Image` draw the tinted pane — edge, contact shadow, rim and glow — when their styling prop `boxShadow` is `"contact"`, the image without rim and glow, which would lie over the picture. The mixin is `contactPane()` of the ground module. A `Section` with `onClick` is drawn and behaves like the filled button whatever `boxShadow` says: the full pane, the interaction edge and veil under the pointer and the focus, the veil laid twice and the shadow pulled together under a press, no lift. Its prop types require a `backgroundColor` or a `backgroundImage`, and it holds no controls.

## Two kinds of shadow

**The contact shadow** belongs to a body lying on a surface — a control's pane, a placed component's pane. It depends on the ground and has a form for a light and one for a dark ground. Its dark-ground values are a compromise: on `primary`, the darkest ground of the palette, it reads faintly, and denser values made it too heavy on every other dark ground.

**The floating shadows** describe a surface that floats above the page with air in between, three of them named after where it sits: `anchored` hangs from its reference (the select-box menus, the mega menu, a card on its anchor), `floating` stands free (a card, a notification, the minimized modwin), `modal` lies above everything else (the modwin, the dialog). They are drawn as over a light ground whatever lies below. The one floating component that follows the ground all the same is the overlaid button: it rests with `anchored` and carries a dark-ground form of it in its own stylesheet.

The check box and the bare button carry no pane at all, and an input control gives its pane up with the prop `bare`; the surrounding layout then does the bounding, a table whose rows are already divided, for instance. A pane-less control keeps its inner spacing all the same, because the interaction veil fills the pane's shape whether the pane is drawn or not.

Every pane is measured from the map: `heightDefault` 30 with `borderRadiusDefault` 15, a pill; `heightLarge` 50 with `borderRadiusLarge`, which carries the same 15 since 2026-09-07 and leaves a control of that height a pane with rounded corners rather than a pill; a radius of 25, the half of `heightLarge`, for the one large control that is a circle, the overlaid icon button. An input control pads its value by `inputControlPaddingLeftRight` (12) on either side and separates value and icons by `inputControlColumnGap` (7). Icons are `iconDimDefault` (18) and `iconDimLarge` (30).

**`flush`** — `'start'`, `'end'` or `'both'` — says that a control ends without an edge of its own on that side. A paned control squares its corners there and drops its border along it, so two controls strung together meet in a seam of nothing but their contact shadows; a bare control pulls its inner spacing back out with a negative margin, so its lettering lines up with what stands above or below it. The values are the logical sides, and a right-to-left document mirrors them by itself.

## The two axes

A control shows two kinds of status at once, and they **add up**: no status hides another, with one exception.

- **The status**, which the consumer sets through the prop `status`, exactly one at a time and `IDLE` until set otherwise. The button carries `IDLE`, `DISABLED`, `BUSY` and `ACTIVE`; the check box and the switch `IDLE` and `DISABLED`; every input control `IDLE`, `DISABLED`, `ERROR` and `BUSY`. A changed value is no status of any control: the form around it states such a thing, through a reset or a save that becomes possible (ADR `general-changed-value-is-no-control-status.md`). `BUSY` and `ACTIVE` work on the filled button alone — on the other forms the component normalizes them to `IDLE` before anything reads them. A select box with nothing left to choose sets `DISABLED` on itself.
- **The interaction statuses**, which the control determines itself and the consumer cannot set: `FOCUS` and `HOVER` on every control, `PRESSED` on the button. They come from the CSS pseudo-classes `:hover` and `:focus-visible` — `:focus-within` on the input group, whose caret has to show whatever put the focus there — not from the flags `useInteractions` reports, which stay public API for a consumer's logic.

The exception is the **lock**: while the status is `DISABLED`, `BUSY` or `ACTIVE`, the control shows no interaction status and takes no input, the cursor is the default one, and the pane thins by one step (see above). The control keeps determining the interaction statuses nonetheless, so `HOVER` returns the moment the lock lifts under a resting pointer.

An interaction status arrives instantly and leaves over 150 ms: the `controls` map holds the pair `interactionEaseInMs: 0` and `interactionEaseOutMs: 150`, the status's rule sets the first, the resting rule the second. A press held for one rendered frame reaches its full appearance and fades afterwards; a status arriving mid-press overlays the fading press. **Do not consolidate the two durations into one** — the asymmetry is the whole mechanism.

Every layer of a control's appearance rides in a **slot**, a CSS custom property, and one `box-shadow` assembles them: `--paneShadow`, `--paneRim`, `--paneGlow` for the pane, `--statusVeil` for the veil, `--statusPress` for the press on the button; the input group adds `--paneFill`, `--paneBorderColor` and `--paneEaseMs`. A status sets its own slot and touches no other, which is what lets the statuses add up. An unused slot holds a shadow of zero size in a transparent colour — `slotEmpty` for an outer slot, `slotEmptyInset` for an inset one, `slotEmptyVeil` for the two-layer veil — never nothing: a shadow list interpolates only while both sides hold the same number of layers, so a slot that empties to nothing jumps instead of easing. A sub-component in a CSS module of its own draws a slot it inherits, the check box's icon its `--statusVeil`, because no selector crosses a module's boundary.

## The interaction veil

`FOCUS` and `HOVER` have **two appearances, and what chooses between them is whether the thing under the pointer has a face at all.** Where it has one — a pane, a check box's box, a calendar day's circle, a tab whose selection is a lens — it takes the veil below. Where a component marks its selection on the lettering instead, its entries have no bounded area, and a veil spread over a text row invents a ground the row never has at rest; such an entry takes the underline of *The interaction underline* below. The tab bar is the one control that shows both, one per marker. Everywhere else the answer follows from the same question: the primary header's nodes take the veil, their selection being a glass marker that grows over the active node; the options of the select box's menu and of the input's proposal list take it as well, a marker covering one row; the entries of the popup `Menu`, the mega menu's nodes and the first sidebar's take the underline, their selection sitting on the lettering. The multi select box's options are check boxes and carry the veil on their box already (ADR `PDWG-83-tab-bar-hover-follows-the-marker.md`).

The veil is the appearance of a face. `FOCUS` and `HOVER` show one thing on it: a **veil of two layers** over the control's face. The lower layer darkens — `primary` at .05 on a light background, `offWhite` at .07 on a dark one — and the upper one is `impulseGreen` at .08 or .10, the interaction colour, which names the darkening as an interaction. `PRESSED` adds the same veil a second time. The veil is an inset shadow spread wide enough to meet itself in the middle of any control, so it lies over whatever is behind it, the pane as much as a saturated `highlight` colour: a red button under the pointer is a red button with a green cast.

**The edge follows the form, not the status.** A control that carries a pane has a line already and colours it `impulseGreen` (.7 on light, .8 on dark) while the veil is up; a control without a pane grows no line. **The face the veil covers is the control itself:** the round box the check box's icon sits in, never its label; the whole pane of an input control, which holds nothing but the value; a tab of the tab bar, rounded like the marker that covers it. Where a control already shows the veil and a part inside it takes the focus — the focused part of the date time picker — that part takes the veil a second time, the sum a pressed button shows. The calendar's days take the same veil on their own face, the round box each number sits in; the options of the select box's menu and the rows of the input's proposal list take it on the row, square like the marker that covers one of them. The multi select box's options are check boxes, which carry the veil on their box, so the row around them adds none. The switch, made for touch-only projects, takes the veil for the focus alone and never for the pointer (ADR `PDWG-87-switch-as-paned-control-for-touch-only-projects.md`).

Selected text is no interaction status. It keeps a neutral highlight, `controls.color.textSelection`, in both themes.

## The interaction underline

The appearance of an entry with no face, and it is the veil's two layers translated to text — each half doing the work its layer does there. The lettering reaches full opacity from `interactionTextOpacity` (.8), which carries the visibility the way the neutral layer does, and `interactionUnderline` — `impulseGreen` at full strength, `interactionUnderlineWidth` 2 at `interactionUnderlineOffset` 3 — names the change as an interaction the way the green layer does. Neither half works alone: the opacity by itself says only "this got stronger", and the line by itself rests on a colour that reaches 1.36:1 against `offWhite`, the measurement that ruled out a focus ring of its own.

**The line fades, it does not wipe.** It is a `text-decoration` whose colour transitions, so it lies exactly as long as the word it marks whatever the caption's box is. The classic text link is the one line that moves: `_nativeElements.scss` gives every `a` a permanent green line that retracts under the pointer, because that line marks the text *as* a link rather than stating an interaction, and an `a` hugs its own text (ADR `general-interaction-underline-fades-and-the-link-wipes.md`).

**The underline takes no theme pair**, unlike the veil's neutral layer and the interaction edge: a line of a saturated colour separates itself from a light and a dark ground alike, where a neutral layer has to know which way to move. Its offset is the one the active menu entry's line carries, so a list whose selection is underlined already shows one line in two colours — `primary` for the selection, `impulseGreen` for the interaction — rather than two lines. A container with no lettering takes the opacity half alone, as the tab bar's container tab does.

Two entries rest at full opacity all the same: the **selected** one, because a marked entry is not a weakened one, and the **disabled** one, whose lettering its disabled typo set has weakened already, so that a second thinning would multiply. The `menuEntry` mixin holds both at it too, and it is the mixin that carries the appearance into the menus: the first sidebar's nodes, the mega menu's nodes and the popup `Menu`'s items show it wherever they are, the mixin stating its lettering in one theme because everything that includes it is light (`dark-areas.md`). **The line sits on a child with the class `caption`**, which is what keeps it off an entry's icons and what an entry made of several parts has; an entry without such a child — the breadcrumbs today — shows the opacity half alone, as the tab bar's container tab does. Where a selection is underlined already, the mixin's `.active` writes `primary` onto the very line the interaction colours, so the hover exchanges the colour instead of adding a second line.

## The status

- **`DISABLED`, `BUSY`, `ACTIVE`** lock the control (see above); its lettering takes `controls.color.disabled` where it is locked.
- **`BUSY`** shows a wait in the form of the control: on the button a light band travelling across the plate once per 1400 ms, carried by a pseudo-element and standing still under `prefers-reduced-motion`; on an input control a spinner in place of the trailing icon.
- **`ACTIVE`** shares the button's `attention` branch — something is switched on, which is notable and uncritical.
- **`ERROR`** colours the edge of an input control `attentionHigh`, in the bare form as well, whose edge is drawn and transparent at rest. `signalError` is never a status of the interface (`colors.md`).
- The **value** keeps its own colour in every status, with one thinning: the fill of a disabled switch that is on drops to the alpha of the disabled lettering, so that it states the value without promising a switch that can be used.
- A **notice** or error text stands below the pane, indented to where the value starts — the inset travels to the helper as `--noticeInset` — and colours itself for `ERROR`.

## Icons

An icon of a control is one path in the colour of its status, and everything inside it is a hole: the inside of an empty box, the tick, the mixed bar, the gap around a radio button's dot. The holes are subpaths wound against the contour enclosing them, so no icon depends on a `fill-rule`. The background shows through, and the veil, lying behind the icon, reaches through it. The tick box's corners are rounded by 4 of its 18 units, a radius drawn into the path so that it scales with the glyph across the two sizes.

## The switch

The switch is the one control that is wider than it is high, and the one whose value CSS draws rather than a glyph: a pane of the tinted strength, 50 wide by `heightDefault` (30) high, with a knob of 22 travelling on it; the two measures of its own stand with their reasons in `switch.scss`. The knob is a body of the base design's glass, placed out of the flow 3 px inside the pane's edge: an `offWhite` veil at .7, the same in every status and theme, so that it lightens whatever lies under it — the grey track as much as the blue one. Its edge and its contact shadow follow the ground like every pane's and are twice as dense as the surface's, because a body of 22 px has to separate from a track of the same glass; rim and glow are the surface's own (`switch.scss`). It moves by its logical inline start over `animationTime.mediumMs`, so a right-to-left document mirrors the travel by itself and no compositing layer is paid for. While the switch is on, the pane fills with `attention` — a setting that is switched on is level 2 of the attention ladder (`colors.md`), the colour the `ACTIVE` button carries for the same statement — and takes the glass of `surfaceColored` (above), while the knob keeps its glass and takes the dark-ground edge and shadow.

The switch serves projects on touch-only devices and for those alone; wherever a pointer or a keyboard is in play, the check box is the control. It takes the interaction veil and the interaction edge for the focus, which a keyboard attached to such a device can still give it, and nothing for the pointer. It has one size: the shared height is what makes the pane large enough for a finger, where the glyph it replaced needed a large size. Its statuses are `IDLE` and `DISABLED`. `DISABLED` thins the pane to `surfaceLocked`, the knob by one step — fill and edge at half, rim and glow at the tinted strength, no shadow — the label to `controls.color.disabled`, and the fill of a switch that is on to the same alpha. Its status slots ride on the root element, where the focus lands and the status classes stand, and the pane and the knob inherit and draw them. The switch keeps its label for the reason the check box does (below).

## The tab bar

The tab bar switches between the contents of one part of a content — as a rule a `Section` set off from the content's ground by its colour — and lies on one of that part's four edges, which its prop `pos` names: above the part (`top`, the default), below it, or beside it, where the tabs stack. A tab is a title with an optional subtitle, `TabBarTitleItem`, or a grid container for any content, `TabBarContrItem`. **The bar's direction decides two things about its tabs.** A bar that lies over or under its content runs along the reading direction: it centres its titles, the way a menu of one level does, and keeps `space xs` (7) between two tabs, which their own inline padding of 12 a side already widens to 31. A bar beside its content stacks them, and a stack of entries is a list: its lettering starts where the reading text starts, so a right-to-left document turns it around by itself, and the gap grows to `space small` (12), because above and below a title is padded by 4 alone. The title tab is a CSS module of its own, so the bar hands both down as slots, `--tabItemJustifyContent` and `--tabItemTextAlign`. The bar shows the selection and nothing more: the consumer holds the selected tab's ID in `selectedId` and sets it from the tabs' `onClick`. Tabs that do not fit scroll, by wheel, by touch and by a scroll button at either end. A tab the selection moves to is scrolled into view clear of the scroll button and of the fade around it, the length of the button's shader (50) on either side.

It has **two appearances**, chosen by the prop `backgroundMarker`, and each belongs to a placement:

- **The lens, the default** — the bar lies *in* the part, on the part's colour, and the selected tab carries a **lens** behind its lettering: a body of the base design's glass lying on the bar, tinted in the marker's colour at an alpha of .3 (`marker/Marker.tsx`). As long as every tab fits, the tabs share the bar's width. This is the look of a menu with a single level, the primary header's. The tint is `attention` unless `markerColor` says otherwise: the colour that says which of several things is the one switched on (`colors.md`), the statement the `ACTIVE` button and the switch that is on make in the same colour.
- **The background marker** — the bar stands *at* the part's edge, on the surrounding ground, and the selected tab is filled, `offWhite` unless `markerColor` says otherwise. The consumer sets `markerColor` to the part's colour, so that the selected tab runs into the content without a seam. The tabs pack at the bar's start, because a filled tab has to end where the tab ends. This is the look of the classic tabs of a desktop program. A filled tab of a dark colour lightens its own lettering, alone among the tabs. The bar itself carries no colour of its own unless `backgroundColor` gives it one.

The lens is the switch knob's construction with a colour instead of the neutral veil: the fill is the marker's colour thinned to a tint, and the glass around it is the **surface's own** — its edge, its lit rim, its inner glow and its contact shadow, unchanged. A translucent tint leaves those ingredients their work, where an opaque fill cancels them and asks for `surfaceColored` instead. The tint is thin enough that the bar's ground reads through the lens, so the selected tab keeps the lettering of the ground it stands on. The lens covers its tab and is rounded by `borderRadiusDefault` (15), which gives it the geometry of a control's pane: a tab is at least `heightDefault` (30) high — the title tab pads its lettering by `space small` (12) to the left and right and by 4 above and below, the largest whole pixel that leaves the minimum reachable, and the container tab keeps the same floor — so the lens of a tab of one line is a pill, and a tab whose content asks for more height carries a taller lens at the same radius. Around the tabs the bar keeps `space xs` (7) of air on the axis across it, the same distance its gap puts between two tabs, and the lens stays inside that air, where its contact shadow has the room to be seen. **The marker of a filled tab reaches over that air** and takes the bar's whole height, which costs no rule: the containing block of an absolutely positioned element is its ancestor's padding box, so an inset of zero already covers the padding, and it is the lens that keeps out of it by an inset of the padding's own size, which the bar hands down as `--tabBarPadding`. Its glass follows the ground the bar lies on, which only the bar knows, so the bar sets the four ingredients as slots — `--markerBorderColor`, `--markerShadow`, `--markerRim`, `--markerGlow` — and the marker, a CSS module of its own, inherits and draws them.

The styling prop `borderRadius` — the one radius prop the bar takes — rounds the two corners that face away from the content, the top corners of a bar above it, in logical corners so that a vertical bar keeps its outer side in a right-to-left document. A background marker takes those two corners as well, reaching the bar's edge as it does; the lens stands inside the bar and keeps its own rounding.

**Hover and focus show one of the two interaction appearances, and the marker chooses which** — because the marker is what decides whether a tab has an area of its own. The bar hands its `backgroundMarker` down to every tab as an injected prop, beside the selection, the tab stop and the ground.

- **The lens, so the veil.** The tabs share the bar's width, each of them a bounded area, and the veil of the base design covers it. No interaction edge goes with it: a tab carries no pane, as the check box and the bare button carry none. The veil lies over whatever is behind the tab, the bar's ground or the lens of the selected tab, which shows through it. Each tab is rounded by the marker's own radius, so the veil takes the shape of the marker it lies on.
- **The background marker, so the underline.** The tabs pack at the bar's start, and an unselected tab is no wider than its lettering — there is no area a veil could cover without inventing one. Such a tab shows the interaction appearance of a text entry instead: the lettering reaches full opacity from `interactionTextOpacity` (.8), and `interactionUnderline` — `impulseGreen` at full strength, `interactionUnderlineWidth` 2 at `interactionUnderlineOffset` 3 — underlines it. The line sits under the title alone, never under the subtitle as well, which would read as two targets. **The container tab takes the opacity alone:** an underline needs a line of text to sit under, and that tab holds whatever the call site put in it.

**The selected tab answers the pointer with nothing** — the lens is the statement, and a veil over it would lay a second translucent layer on one tab, which is what the click makes visible while the lens travels onto the tab under the pointer. The focus is excepted and keeps its veil there: it is the only mark a focused tab carries, and the bar's tab stop sits on the selected tab (ADR `general-marker-carrier-shows-no-interaction-veil.md`). The same holds for the primary header's nodes, whose marker is a lens of this base design as well — built from the surface's ingredients in the dark-ground set, with a colourless fill, because the attention belongs to the content and not to the bar that says where one stands (ADR `PDWG-98-primary-header-marker-is-a-colourless-lens.md`). Under the underline appearance two tabs rest at full opacity all the same: the selected one, because a marked entry is not a weakened one and it stands on the opaque marker; and the disabled one, whose lettering the disabled typo set has weakened already, so that a second thinning would multiply.

**The bar is one stop of the tab sequence, not one per tab**, which is what the ARIA tabs pattern asks for. The tab key reaches the selected tab, or the first usable tab where the selection is unset or disabled; the arrow keys then move from tab to tab along the bar's axis and carry the focus with them, `Home` and `End` jump to its two ends, and a disabled tab is passed by. **The selection follows the focus:** an arrow key reports the new tab through that tab's own `onClick`, the callback a click on it would have called, because a tab bar switches a content that is rendered either way. In a right-to-left document the horizontal pair swaps, the first tab lying on the right. **The link to the panel is two props, one per side**, because the bar never sees the panel: the consumer renders it. A tab takes the panel's HTML ID in `panelId` and writes it to `aria-controls`, so that moving to the tab says what it opens; the panel — a `Section`, a `Tabular`, a `Toolbar` or a `DataTable` — takes the tab's ID in `tabBarItemId` and turns into `role="tabpanel"` with `aria-labelledby` on that tab, so that reading the panel says which tab it belongs to. A panel that scrolls carries both on its outer element, the one the scrolling wraps it in, where its own ID sits as well. Setting one side without the other leaves the pair half spoken, and a panel that is a `Section` with an `onClick` is announced as a panel rather than as a button.

The bar reads its ground the way every control does, and a `backgroundColor` of its own sets it for the tabs. The tab a filled marker covers stands on that marker's colour and takes its ground. The marker slides from one tab to the next over `animationTime.slowMs` when the selection moves and appears in place otherwise: on the first render, and when a tab changes its size or the bar its direction. It is placed by its inset, never by a `transform`, so that its edges are snapped to the device pixel like the content's and a filled tab meets its content without a seam (ADR `PDWG-83-tab-bar-marker-placed-by-inset.md`).

## Labels

An input control carries no label of its own. The layout names it, in a track beside the controls': a `Section` with `gridTemplateColumns="auto 1fr"` and `alignItems="baseline"`, the labels in the first track and the controls in the second, puts every pane of a column on one edge and gives it one width, however long the labels are — `proj/contents/examples/login/loginMask/LoginMask.jsx` is the pattern. The control exports the baseline the label aligns against: a grid container takes its baseline from its first item in document order, that item is the value, and its line box is as tall as the pane's **inside** — the pane's height less its two edges — which puts the baseline in the pane's middle and the lettering with it. The input group needs no declaration for that, its value being the first item. The button needs two: its label asks for the row's baseline with `align-self: baseline`, because an icon may stand before it and an SVG has no baseline to give, and a button carrying no lettering at all holds an empty span that does nothing but carry the same line box. Without that span such a button hands out a baseline synthesized from its icon's lower edge and stands 2.6 px above a text beside it, 8.6 px at the large height. The check box holds the same span for the same reason.

The check box and the switch keep their label — `label`, `labelType`, `labelFirst`, `wrapLabel` — because their text is their content rather than a name for it. With `labelFirst` set, a stretched check box or switch pushes label and icon or pane to its two edges, so a column of them named on the left carries its icons or panes on one edge; `justifySelf="start"` at the call site takes that back.

## The popup worlds

The menus of the select boxes, the input's proposal list and the date time picker's calendar are surfaces, not controls: **they are light whatever they cover** (`dark-areas.md`), and they stand on the opaque glass of `glassmorphism($strength: opaque)` with the floating shadow `anchored` in `--glassShadow`, the one a surface hanging from its trigger casts, and the rounding `controlMenus.borderRadius` (12) — the two menus as elements of their own, the proposal list and the calendar through the `Card`. An option is `controlMenus.optionHeight` tall, which equals `heightDefault`, so the option lying on the control covers it exactly; the option's line box is two pixels taller, which answers the pane's two edges.

A popup **computes its height** — options that fit the room the viewport leaves, header rows, the glass edge counted twice, `controlMenus.spaceToDocument` (5) kept to the viewport's edge — and is placed against the **drawn edge** of the pane, what `getBoundingClientRect()` returns, corrected for nothing and rounded nowhere: the option's text lands on the value's text, and where a negative margin has pulled a pane past its column, the popup follows it. A menu moves by `transform`, which animates the selection change and costs a one-device-pixel jump on scaled displays. A card whose height the layout cannot give it — the data table's columns selection card — measures its own content and states the height itself: a scrolling section contributes no height of its own.

## Verifying a control

The playground content, `proj/contents/examples/playground/`, is the repo's test bed: its select box switches the background through every colour of the palette that can be one, and a control under judgement goes in for as long as it is judged and comes out afterwards. A pass over the 13 backgrounds — the palette's 15 colours less `invisible`, two of them repeating a value — in every status and under the pointer is what accepts a control's appearance. Two things to judge beside the control itself: the same veil on a small face, a check box's box, and the statuses in both themes, since a rule that looks right in one theme is finished only in the other.

Alignment is measured, not argued. `Range.selectNodeContents(el)` plus `getBoundingClientRect().top` gives the top of the glyph box — baseline minus ascent — rather than the line box, so two texts in the same lettering are on one baseline exactly when the values are equal, in different elements too. Measure a popup's text against the control's with the popup open and with it shut: an open popup can move the pane, and a comparison in one of the two is blind to it.
